title_ar: من جر ثوبه خيلاء لم ينظر الله إليه يوم القيامة
title_en: Whoever Trails His Garment out of Pride, God Will Not Look at Him on the Day of Resurrection
body_ar:
سؤال عن قوله صلى الله عليه وسلم«من جر ثوبه خيلاء لم ينظر الله إليه يوم القيامة» فهل هذا مختص بالخيلاء أم لا؟ إن الأصوليين اختلفوا في ما جاء مطلقا من الشارع ثم جاء مقيدا هل يحمل المطلق على المقيد أو يبقى المطلق على إطلاقه و المقيد على قيده فمن أمثلة ذلك قول الله تعالى في كفارة الظهار﴿فتحرير رقبة من قبل أن يتماسا﴾ فلم يشرط فيها الإسلام فجعلها مطلقة وفي كفارة القتل قال﴿فتحرير رقبة مؤمنة﴾ فشرط فيها الإسلام فهل يحمل المطلق على المقيد فكل رقبة لا بد فيها من الإسلام أو يبقى المطلق على إطلاقه فكفارة الظهار يمكن أن تكون غير مسلمة و كفارة القتل لا بد فيها من الإسلام هذا محل خلاف بين الأصوليين

وقد صح عن النبي صلى الله عليه و سلم فيما يتعلق بالإسبال إطلاق و تقييد أما الإطلاق فقوله صلى الله عليه وسلم«ما أسفل من الكعبين في النار» و أما التقييد فقوله «من جر ثوبه خيلاء» فقد قيد ذلك بالخيلاء فحمل ذلك بعض أهل العلم على التقييد فرأوا أن الإسبال من غير خيلاء لا يتوعد صاحبه بهذا الوعيد و استدلوا بقول أبي بكر رضي الله عنه إن إزاري يسترخي فقال«لست منهم» فأبو بكر يسترخي إزاره لكنه مع ذلك لم يفعل ذلك خيلاء فقال له النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم«لست منهم» ويفهم من هذا أن من فعل ذلك من غير خيلاء لا يكون متوعدا بهذا الوعيد لكن الإحتياط أن لا يسبل الإنسان مطلقا فقد رأي النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم رجلا يصلي في الحرم مسبلا فأمره أن يعيد الصلاة والطهارة فجعل ذلك ناقضا للوضوء ومبطلا للصلاة فلذلك لا بد أن يحرص الإنسان على عدم الإسبال و الإنسان الذي يعرف أن أكفانه ضيقة و أنها تكفيه و هي نصيبه من هذه الحياة الدنيا عليه أن يعلم أن الإسبال في الثياب والزيادة فيها تجاوز الرصغ مثلا في (الدراعة) أو تجاوز الإبهام ومثل ذلك تجاوز الكعب فيها لا خير فيه بوجه من الوجوه فهذا أمير المؤمنين عمر رضي الله عنه و وقد طعن عند موته مر بين يديه شاب من الأنصار قد أسبل ثوبه فدعاه فقال ردوه علي فقال إرفع ثوبك فإنه أتقى و أنقى و أبقى فهو أتقى لله و أنقى للثوب وأطهر له وأبقى له أيضا حتى لا يتعرض للتلف وقد صح في حديث بن عمر رضي الله عنهما أنه مر أمام حجرة حفصة فرآه رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم فدعاه فقال«إرفع إزارك قال فرفعته ثم قال زد فزدت ثم قال زد فزدت» فلما سكت جرح بن عمر ساقه من ذلك المكان حتى يعرف المكان الذي أذن رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم في بلوغ الإزار إليه.

-----------------------------------------------------------------

معيار تمييز الحق من الباطل

لقد كثرت الفرق التي تدعي أنها على الحق وأن غيرها على الباطل فما العمل بالنسبة لها؟

أن الله تعالى يقول: {يَا أَيُّهَا الَّذِينَ آَمَنُوا إِنْ تَتَّقُوا اللَّهَ يَجْعَلْ لَكُمْ فُرْقَانًا وَيُكَفِّرْ عَنْكُمْ سَيِّئَاتِكُمْ} [الأنفال 29] والفرقان الواضح أن المعيار الذي لدينا هو ما جاء به محمد (ص)، فما كان موافقا لما جاء به محمد (ص) فهو الحق الذي لا مرية فيه، وما كان مخالفا له فهو مردود على صاحبه «من عمل عملا ليس عليه أمرنا فهو رد»، «من أحدث في أمرنا هذا ما ليس منه فهو رد».
body_en:
A question about his words, peace and blessings be upon him: 'Whoever trails his garment out of pride, God will not look at him on the Day of Resurrection.' Is this restricted to pride or not?

The legal theorists differed over what comes from the Lawgiver unqualified (muṭlaq) and then comes qualified (muqayyad): whether the unqualified is to be carried to the qualified, or whether the unqualified remains in its unqualified state and the qualified in its qualification. An example of this is the words of God, exalted, concerning the expiation for the oath of separation: {then the freeing of a slave, before the two of them touch one another} (Sūrat al-Mujādilah 58:3) — where He did not stipulate Islam in it, so He left it unqualified. And concerning the expiation for killing He said: {then the freeing of a believing slave} (Sūrat al-Nisāʾ 4:92) — where He did stipulate Islam in it. So is the unqualified to be carried to the qualified, so that every slave must be a Muslim; or does the unqualified remain in its unqualified state, so that the expiation for the oath of separation may be a non-Muslim, while the expiation for killing must be a Muslim? This is a place of disagreement among the legal theorists.

It is soundly established from the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, that in what concerns the letting down of the garment (isbāl) there is both an unqualified text and a qualified one. As for the unqualified: his words, peace and blessings be upon him, 'What is below the ankles is in the Fire.' And as for the qualified: his words, 'Whoever trails his garment out of pride' — he qualified that with pride. Some of the people of knowledge carried the matter to the qualification, and held that one who lets down his garment without pride is not threatened with this threat. They adduced as evidence the words of Abu Bakr, God be pleased with him: 'My lower garment slips down' — and he said: 'You are not one of them.' So Abu Bakr's lower garment did slip down, but along with that he did not do it out of pride, and the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said to him: 'You are not one of them.' It is understood from this that one who does it without pride is not threatened with this threat.

But the precautionary course is that a person should not let his garment down at all. For the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, saw a man praying in the Sacred Precinct with his garment let down, and commanded him to repeat the prayer and the purification, making that a nullifier of the ablution and an invalidator of the prayer. For that reason a person must be careful to avoid letting the garment down. And the person who knows that his shroud is narrow, and that it suffices him, and that it is his portion of this lower life, ought to know that letting the garments down and adding to them — going beyond the wrist, for instance, in the dirrāʿah, or going beyond the thumb; and likewise going beyond the ankle in them — has no good in it in any respect whatever. Here is the Commander of the Faithful ʿUmar, God be pleased with him: when he had been stabbed, at his death, a young man of the Ansar passed before him with his garment let down, and he called him, and said: 'Bring him back to me.' And he said: 'Raise your garment, for it is more God-fearing, and cleaner, and longer-lasting' — that is, more God-fearing towards God, and cleaner for the garment and purer for it, and also longer-lasting for it, so that it is not exposed to ruin. And it is soundly established in the hadith of Ibn ʿUmar, God be pleased with them both, that he passed in front of the chamber of Hafsah and the Messenger of God, peace and blessings be upon him, saw him and called him and said: 'Raise your lower garment.' He said: So I raised it. Then he said: 'More.' So I did more. Then he said: 'More.' So I did more. And when he fell silent, Ibn ʿUmar made a mark on his shin at that place, so that he would know the place up to which the Messenger of God, peace and blessings be upon him, had permitted the lower garment to reach.

-----------------------------------------------------------------

The criterion for distinguishing truth from falsehood

The sects that claim to be upon the truth and that others are upon falsehood have become many. What is to be done about them?

God, exalted, says: {O you who believe, if you are conscious of God, He will give you a criterion and will efface your bad deeds from you} (Sūrat al-Anfāl 8:29). And the criterion, plainly, is that the standard we have is what Muhammad, peace and blessings be upon him, brought. Whatever agrees with what Muhammad, peace and blessings be upon him, brought is the truth in which there is no doubt; and whatever contradicts it is thrown back on the one who does it: 'Whoever performs an act that our affair is not in accordance with, it is rejected'; 'Whoever introduces into this affair of ours something that is not of it, it is rejected.'

flags.arabic: لكن الإحتياط أن لا يسبل الإنسان مطلقا
flags.context: the Sheikh's own position, after reporting the view of 'some of the people of knowledge'
options: the precautionary course is that a person should not let his garment down at all
it is obligatory not to let the garment down at all
it is forbidden to let the garment down at all
flags.note: CRITICAL — THE RULING-STRENGTH POINT OF THE WHOLE RECORD. The Sheikh never declares the letting down of the garment forbidden, and he never resolves the usul disagreement he opened with between carrying the unqualified to the qualified and leaving each in place. What he says is that the precautionary course (al-iḥtiyāṭ) is to avoid it entirely, and that there is no good in it. That is counsel of precaution, not a ruling of prohibition, and this is one of the most contested questions in contemporary fiqh precisely over that distinction. Options 2 and 3 would put a ruling in his mouth that he deliberately withheld.

flags.arabic: فقد رأي النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم رجلا يصلي في الحرم مسبلا فأمره أن يعيد الصلاة والطهارة فجعل ذلك ناقضا للوضوء ومبطلا للصلاة
flags.context: the report the Sheikh adduces for the precautionary position
options: render as the Sheikh gives it, with no grading, and flag
render and note that the report's grading is disputed
flags.note: IMPORTANT. This is by far the strongest claim in the record — that letting the garment down nullifies the ablution and invalidates the prayer — and the Sheikh gives it with no narrator, no collection and no grading, in a record where he has twice said of other reports that they are soundly established. The grading of this particular report is contested in the hadith literature. Nothing has been supplied in either direction, but a reviewer should note the contrast: the English reader has no way of seeing that the Sheikh graded two reports here and not this one.

flags.arabic: تجاوز الرصغ مثلا في (الدراعة) أو تجاوز الإبهام
flags.context: the Sheikh's examples of excess in garments
options: going beyond the wrist, for instance, in the dirrāʿah, or going beyond the thumb
going beyond the wrist in the robe, or beyond the thumb's length
flags.note: DIALECT AND LOCAL DRESS. The dirrāʿah, given in round brackets in the source, is the wide Mauritanian gown; the brackets suggest the site's editors also felt the word needed marking. The two measurements — beyond the wrist and beyond the thumb — refer to the sleeve and are not explained, so what exactly is being measured is not recoverable from the text. Left as the Arabic has it, with nothing supplied. A reviewer familiar with Mauritanian dress should gloss this.

flags.arabic: هل يحمل المطلق على المقيد … هذا محل خلاف بين الأصوليين
flags.context: the legal-theory frame the Sheikh opens with
options: preserve the whole usul argument and leave the disagreement unresolved
compress the argument to its application
state which side the Sheikh takes
flags.note: CRITICAL FOR DISPLAY. The Sheikh frames the whole question as an instance of a general usul problem, illustrates it with the two expiation verses, and explicitly says it is a place of disagreement among the legal theorists. He then never says which side he takes. The reasoning chain must be preserved and not compressed into a conclusion, and the English must not let his closing counsel of precaution read as an answer to the theoretical question. The glossary's renderings for muṭlaq and muqayyad have been used throughout.

flags.context: two unrelated fatwas served under one title
options: flag as compound and let the site present the two separately
flags.note: The page carries a second and entirely unrelated fatwa, on the criterion for distinguishing truth from falsehood among competing sects, under its own heading and separated by a rule of hyphens. It is invisible from the record's title. Not split unilaterally; the site should present the two as distinct items.

Qur'anic and hadith renderings in this file are interpretive translations of meaning, offered to carry the Sheikh's argument in English. They are not a substitute for the Arabic.

The Qur'anic quotations in the first section are given without references; the references have been supplied per house style. The quotation in the second section carries its sūrah name and verse number in the source.
'The oath of separation' renders ẓihār, the pre-Islamic formula of repudiation addressed in Sūrat al-Mujādilah; it is not in the glossary and should be added.
'The letting down of the garment' renders isbāl, the wearing of a garment below the ankles, which is the subject of the whole first section; it is not in the glossary and should be added.

'More God-fearing, and cleaner, and longer-lasting' renders ʿUmar's rhymed triplet atqā / anqā / abqā, followed by his own gloss of each term, which the Sheikh reproduces; the rhyme has not been attempted in English, per the house rule.
The source spells الإحتياط with connecting hamza, رأي for رأى, and بن عمر for ابن عمر; all preserved in body_ar.
